Generous with their time and knowledge, especially those of you trying to break into the industry full time. 

A good year, more work to be done. I kind of have a bad feeling about 2026...

Finally I would like to thank everyone this year who interacted with me on stocks, especially those of you significantly wealthier and more short on time than myself for being generous with your time. I am extremely thankful for fellow young investors who have also been very....

The rest of my holdings, up to 10 in total this year, are microcaps. I will continue to put a large portion of my portfolio into small companies. I will be posting a write up this week in the usual place reviewing my year more in depth and going into my microcap holdings.

$VTY.L are basically flat for me on the year. I would expect the following year to be more eventful and hopefully more reflective of the tailwinds benefitting the company over the coming years. Happy to continue to hold.

I am not naive enough to expect a linear path forward, especially given recent history, but the year's developments have given me renewed reasons to continue holding the company and allow the story to continue to play out. I am up around 32% on my position as of writing.

$BFIT, after a significant period of being dead money for me, finally seems to be gaining some traction. The company this year announced the acquisition of a German franchise chain and Covid era club openings appear to be improving economics more in line with legacy gyms

It may take time but my personal view is that shares at current prices present a very attractive risk reward profile for new investors and the company is also a victim of negativity around microcap UK stocks. It's trading at 6-7x trough earnings, 3x EV/EBITDA.

On $CHH.L - I will be stubborn on this one, possibly to my detriment. The company's poor trading post Covid has been blamed on a weak hospitality industry and increasing energy prices. Before making a final judgment on this, I need to see one, or both of these headwinds subside.

Despite this, I am more pleased with my ability to identify and buy into an exceptional opportunity. I did my work on Nordrest largely in a bubble before later learning of it's favour amongst some bigger fish. I hope to hold it for a long time and may yet add on a bad Q results.

I am once again satisfied with my years work. Mistakes were made but luckily I made more good decisions than bad ones. A large regret of mine is that I did not size up Nordrest far larger and was too stubborn on price anchoring for a company I had very high conviction on.

Will release my 2026 predictions next week, but here's a sneak peak on where I see the broader US market heading... S&P approaches the 8500 range. 

While that may seem very bullish, it's actually just a call that we approach the upper end of the upward trading channel that we have been in for the better part of the last twenty years. (See monthly SPX chart below.)

While a basic and simple chart, I think it tells a profound story. We created an upward trend line from the Oct. 2007 monthly-close high to the Dec 2021 monthly-close high. 

Earlier this year, we bumped up against it in Q1 and rejected hard, the so-called tariff tantrum. But we rallied back up strong and broke through it in September. Then we checked back down to it in November and are now back firmly above it at new highs. 

Big picture: I see the blue parallel channel as the new uptrend, which should get us approaching 8500 by end of 2026. I see the former resistance line (orange below) created by the 2007 & 2021 highs as new support.

If you're looking for a range on where silver takes a breather, I'm looking at $81.985 to $88.0229 as where this thing pauses. 

Going by April 2011 Monthly high close of $47.912 minus the Dec. 2015 Monthly low close of $13.839 gets a spread of $34.073. That spread plus the April '11 monthly close of $47.912 gives you $81.985. 

If you use intraday high and low, you got up to $49.831 in APR '11 and down to $11.6391 in March '20 for a spread of $38.1919. That spread plus the high gives you $88.0229.

From there, I'd be looking for up to a 50% retracement of that spread to the mid-$60s for the next buying opportunity.

17) I like to see that insiders own a significant portion of the company. It’s not a must, but it’s clearly an advantage when insiders have skin in the game.
16) The market is usually slow to price in good and bad reports, which creates opportunities if you’re quick to react.

15) I avoid companies with large net debt, as it increases the risk in the case, and there’s a chance the company will have to raise new money through an equity issuance, leading to the risk of dilution.
14) If the valuation becomes too high based on my next-twelve-months estimates, I trim the position or sell entirely.

13) I usually have between 8–12 companies in my portfolio. This creates less volatility than having, say, 5–6 companies, and it gives me more flexibility to adjust weightings in my holdings depending on conviction and valuation.
12) If a company reports a very bad quarter, the next quarters are usually also bad. Therefore, it often proves to be a good idea to sell on bad reports/news.
as they can invest more in R&D, brand, and service than smaller competitors.

11) I prefer small niche companies that are market leaders in their small niche. Becoming a market leader can create advantages like pricing power, and it also makes it easier to widen the moat against competitors
10) I prefer companies that focus on organic growth, and possibly small bolt-on acquisitions that complement the core business. Companies driven by inorganic growth are often too risky.
In rare cases, I might invest in these if the upside versus risk looks very favorable.

9) I prefer companies that are not heavily affected by macroeconomic cycles. The reason is that I don’t have the competence to time those cycles, so I generally avoid investing in banks, oil companies, property developers, and mining companies.
I have positions that have grown to 30–35% of the portfolio because they have increased revenue and EBIT over many years, while the valuation hasn’t become too high.

8) “Let your winners run.” I believe more in averaging up in stocks than averaging down. When I find an attractive stock, I usually build a 3–10% position based on my conviction. If the company proves itself over time, I buy more.

7) I prefer simple business models that are easy to understand, preferably with recurring revenue or relatively predictable revenue. I generally avoid companies that fluctuate a lot from quarter to quarter in revenue, though there can be exceptions.

5) I like to invest in companies where I can find alternative data that gives me an edge over most other investors.

4) I don’t mind paying a relatively high multiple if the quality is sufficiently high. By quality, I mean companies with a strong track record, an excellent business model (e.g., SaaS), good future prospects, and strong moats.

I'm afraid we are feeding/creating a generation (or two) of complainers, whiners, and brats. 

Life is not easy. 

From Buddha to Christ to the Old Testament, life is hard.  Human nature is flawed. You give people a bunch of free stuff, they take advantage, not take a hand up. 

To put it more simply, "It's a jungle out there."

My wife says I suffer from early onset of Grumpy Old Man syndrome, at 50 years old, maybe I do.

But look, I'm sorry if you were told your masters degree in Russian literature from Brown would produce a nice life and now it's not. 

You were fed a bunch of BS lies about education, etc. The reality is, society rewards tangible efforts to increase standards of living.

The WSJ just ran an article about electricians making over 1/4 million a year, riding around data center job sites in golf carts & supervising employees... with huge bonuses to boot. The guy they focused on in the article says, "he pinches himself everyday."

This is still the land of opportunity despite some mean reversion going on. 

The US was 50% of world GDP in the 50s and still we had a hugely bifurcated economy. Racial segregation was rampant. Women were not even considered for consequential roles. 

The US is still the best place to be with the most opportunity, but as always, simply playing it safe won't cut it.

I have to admit. I don't like telling people if they make under $140/year they are poor. It's all a money issue and with some policy changes we can change your life.

I think that a very select group of Americans, namely white, male, native-born heterosexual Christians had basically everything handed to them post WWII. 

You could literally fit into that class of people, be an idiot who barely graduated from HS, and go work 40-hours/week at a factory somewhere and live a great life.

But that was an illusion. A moment in time for a select group. It is not how life generally works.

How life generally works going back hundreds of years is like a pyramid. This is perhaps why all ancient cultures built pyramids. 

There is a huge base of poverty that enables a level of wealth at the top. It has been the same for millenia. It has not changed. And it still exists.

The best place in the world to move from that base to the top tiers has been, is, and likely will continue to be the US.

But if we tell all our young people that you are screwed. That you are just boomer-victims. Then they will start to believe that and demand that which they are not entitled to.

Take a chance. Risk something. Start a business. Leave the safety and comfort of your $100K/year job to make something of yourselves. 

Don't just sit around saying that everything is stacked against you. That life sucks. Poor you.

Then I started it this week, pretty good. 

Also, very close to my time. I turned 10 in 1985, and most of the kids in STs turned about 13 or 14 then; so basically, it’s my age. A simpler age.

An age before social media and YouTube.

As I’ve mentioned before, I never was on any social media until a year or two ago. I’ve found it to be destructive, short-minded, naïve, depressing, and overly cliché.

So, I’m going to take a break and focus on a piece of substance.

I call it my “Monetary Manifesto.”

This is going to be a long-form piece, maybe 50 pages or so, in the spirt of “Common Sense” by Thomas Paine.

The main theses are these:

· We are in a calamitous time, as always… and I stress as always. Civilization always exists on the brink.

· There is an upward trajectory. It did not begin in 1776. It began with the Big Bang billions of years ago. Atoms constantly have been realigning themselves for billions of years into more and more complex organizations, eventually leading to human consciousness.

· This process, that has been on going for billions of years, is not suddenly going to end in 2025.

· Thus, the right bet is on further upward movement, expecting and anticipating dips along the way; dips that are to be bought.

Secondary and more relevant theses are:

· We are in a fundamentally different time than, say, the 1920s. It was a gold standard time and deflation was a reality. This is no longer the case.

· Stocks, in particular, have become a national Ponzi-scheme that must be protected.

· Worries and predictions of a massive collapse are not only wrong, but very harmful to those susceptible.

· Vulnerable people hear calls for Doom & Gloom and then sell or refuse to buy appreciating assets, thus limiting their participation in the modern economy.

· While there have been short-term dips in aggregate wealth, GDP, and wages, the overwhelming trend has been upwards, and there is no sign that is going to end anytime soon.

· Social Media fosters a dark, victim mentality, one which refutes the power of the individual to achieve success. This is perhaps the darkest and most ugly aspect of Doom Scrolling, etc. It leads people to give-up and give-in.

· The ultimate reality is one of opportunity, but too many live in fear and ignorance of the abundance around them.

We all have an amazing future ahead of us.

A Respectful Open Post to All the Doom & Gloomer Pussies

I’m 50 years old. As of two years ago, I had never spent time on any social media--none. 

I just never participated. 

Then I wrote a book called Quoz, about a future where AI and Quantum computing ruled the world, https://t.co/jLMdOPzkSr.

My distributor, @simonschuster,  suggested I get on social media; so I did, never expecting anyone to follow me. 

Within a year or two, I got over 35K followers somehow, I really don’t know why.

But here’s what I’ve learned. Fuck all the, “I’m optimistic at heart, but…” people.

Either you’re an optimist or not. Either you think we’re heading for better days, or you don’t.

I’m beginning to work on a longer, mini-manifesto that I call “The Good, the Bad, & the Ugly.”

The “good” is all the possibility that is around us at this moment in time. It’s AI, humanoids, the breakdown of racial/ethnic barriers to advancement (& I'm not woke but a DJT voter).

The “bad” is the undeniable setbacks that we need to overcome… and overcome them we will… things like large sovereign debt, social wealth inequality, etc.

But the most interesting to me, and the most important for success, is overcoming the “Ugly.” 

The Ugly is all the people on social media and elsewhere that want to convince everyone that they are victims… victims of racism, sexism, generationalism, etc.

These are the people that constantly put out videos/pods on YouTube about the coming collapse, “Worse than the Depression,” the “Markets Set for Massive Meltdown” people, etc. And yes, @thoughtfulmoney, I'm talking about you. I will not hesitate to name names. 

I know this is not a popular view. The popular view is that through some magic of the printing press, the powers that be have forced everyone into a death spiral that will end badly.

I want to push back against this narrative. Attitude is everything. If everyone starts believing they are just victims of circumstance, and that in the end, everything will end in collapse, then that belief becomes toxic.

I also firmly believe that that belief is categorically wrong.

I’m hoping to publish by Jan a well-reasoned and thoughtful piece that confronts all the bad attitudes out there. That promotes optimism without a but.

I was pretty down last week as my “optimistic” portfolio hit a snag. 

Then, I had the best week, on an absolute dollar amount of my life, up over $300K.

Do not let the Doomers get you down. We are on an upward trajectory. It is only a matter of perspective.

All the Puritanical regret about wealth creation is an abomination. 

It is a deep-seated attempt to make people feel bad about making money.

It is a denial of the world and the way it is, a hopeful wish for some puritanical world of fair and justness that simply does not exist.

Follow that philosophy at you're own peril!

A Respectful Counterpoint to Professor Plum

We are living in the most abundant, egalitarian, and luxurious time of human history. However, many are misconstruing a slight dip in white, European-descendant, male-supremacy and -luxury as an overall decline in the U.S./civilization’s upward trend.

I strongly disagree with the premise that we are now worse off than in the 1950s insofar as poverty is concerned.

@profplum99 wrote a thoughtful and well-researched piece about the poverty line. As he notes, it was constructed in the 1960s. He notes that the real poverty line at this point in time should be well over $100K. 

Perhaps. 

However, I would note the following: During the 1950s the U.S. also had a very bifurcated, k-shaped economy despite the misconception that it was a time of abundance for all.

In reality, it was a time of segregation. Immense wealth and opportunity gaps existed both racially and regionally. Indeed, according to historical estimates by the U.S. Census Bureau and economist Gordon Fisher, about 22%–25% of Americans lived below what would later be defined as the poverty line during the late 1950s. This compares to an official poverty rate of 10.6% in the U.S. for 2024.

Prof Plum puts a relevant chart showing this decline in the "official" poverty rate into his piece (linked/copied below). 

But let me not argue that we are better off than the 1950s, but that we are mostly in the same area. 

I think I can make that point. 

And moreover, I think I could make the point that we are mostly in the same area as we were in the 1850s, the 1750s, and indeed the 1550s.

In other words, my counterpoint to Prof Plum is that we are basically where we have been for 100s of years. There really has not been much improvement one way or the other of the societal/caste pyramid.

The difference now is that for the first time ever, the U.S. pyramid is not dominated by white, male, native-born people. 

A fifth-generation American man can now walk down the streets of the Fremont neighborhood in Seattle and see a 26-year-old Chinese-immigrant woman on a visa making twice his annual salary as she leaves her Google or Meta offices.

Does that piss that white guy off? Hell yeah it does. But does that mean that our society is now falling into irreputable disrepair. I think not.

Indeed, I think we are on the verge of actually fulfilling the dream of Jefferson: that all men (women) were created equal. We are on the verge of shifting the historical pyramid of society that goes back centuries. 

But it is always darkest before the dawn.

Do not let the Doom & Gloomers get you down! Do not get mired in the negativity and pessimism of folks like Prof Plum and @adamtaggert.

We are on the verge of greatness. We are correcting past wrongs and paving a pathway towards abundance.

Technology, AI, humanoids, indeed all the blessings that God has provided for us are now finally starting to be harnessed. 

Energy, compute, intelligence, all is before us. Do not let some envious or puritanical-bent get you into the grey.

I’ll give an example. A week or two ago I actually listened to the entire conversation between Prof Plum and Adam Taggert on Thoughtful Money. 

It was all doom and gloom, very sad, and then, incredibly, the outlook of Prof Plum on equities is that their path is higher—but he was somehow disappointed by this because he thought it was driven by passive flows.

What’s more, Adam openly admitted that he been involved in tech back in the day, then left it, and has now seen people of mediocre ability become immensely richer than he because of GOOG or NVDA stock options and that he was jealous. 

In other words, the whole show was the two of them saying stocks are going higher, but we are sad (Greene) and jealous (Taggert) about it. 

What?? 

What the hell is that???

Look, I just watched the whole Ken Burns' “Revolution” series this past week. 

Here’s a reality check: The world has never been fair. There have always been and still currently is a huge percentage of the population living in poverty. 

Perhaps, in the ‘50s, if you just focused on white people in the U.S., it seemed like a utopian time had occurred. 

But go ask the black man, grandson of slaves in Durham, NC if the 1950s were a great time to live.

The global pyramid of supremacy is being rewritten. 

I just listened to an interview on Bloomberg last night with the CEO of FoxCom. He was asked about manufacturing in the U.S. and what the biggest challenge is. 

His response: shortage of workers, not of bodies, but of people who are willing and able to do the work demanded. 

That FoxCom CEO went on to say he knows he needs to work with local and federal governments to get the people trained up and ready to go.

This is going to happen. It will take time, but the overall trajectory of U.S. population standard of living is rising. One in five children used to never see their 5th birthday just a short time ago in the broad span of human history. 

The difference today is that some white folks with college degrees are no longer in the “favored” class. 

Blaming things on index investing or fiat currency is in my mind a cop out. We are working through huge inequalities that have existed in all human societies for centuries. 

It’s just now race/gender aren’t clear definers of economic potential. Overall levels of poverty are mostly in line with long-run historical averages, if not, they are lower and going lower every day. More people around the world are getting healthcare, eating protein, having dental care, etc. than ever before. 

Go back to the ‘50s. There were plenty of black/brown/recent immigrant neighborhoods just a mile or two from the Loop in Chicago to be found without running water, rampant diseases, and overall horror. 

This is the history of America. 

A wealthy country filled with struggling poor; however, now some entitled whites find themselves in the poverty mix. 

We can and will do better, but let us not delude ourselves into thinking we are now in some much worse place than we were 70 or 170 years ago. 

We are in a better place and getting better every day.

Lastly, as I mentioned, the 1950s had huge swaths of poverty and inequality. Eventually these disparities led to social upheaval and massive cultural changes during the 1960s, but they were able to coexist during a time of spectacular stock market performance. 

The S&P turned out an average annual total return of 20.45% over the course of the 1950s, much better performance than the 1920s or even the 1990s could produce. And there was no dot-com bust or Great Depression as the calendar turned to 1960.

Unfortunately, the world is full of a history of a multitude of poor struggling to survive while the wealthy live lives of luxury. 

For most of U.S. history, a strict racial and ethnic segregation protected certain classes. 

Those protections have deteriorated in recent decades, leading many in those historically-protected classes to see the U.S. as on a downward trend. 

However, in the aggregate, irrespective of race or ethnic-background, that is just not the case.

Let’s continue the upward trend, rather than decry a false decline.

Like today, the 1950s were a time when inflation reared its head numerous times, often violently, including a spike to over 20% early in the decade. It was also a time of massive infrastructure buildout, most notably the U.S. interstate system of highways. While data centers and the grid are not the same thing as a highway system, there are similarities. Also reminiscent of the ‘50s is U.S. geopolitical posture. What’s more, the U.S. also had a very bifurcated, k-shaped economy during the ‘50s, despite the misconception that it was a time of abundance for all. It was in reality a time of segregation. Immense wealth and opportunity gaps existed both racially and regionally. OpenAI is trying to break into a very small club, and it has no moats. None. Gemini, XAi, Anthropic, and even Llama all have better positioning. Though Meta/Llama may be most questionable.

This removal of OpenAI as a major player can explain coherently all recent moves of Mag7. Let's take them 1 by 1:

-Google - Gemini and google now seen as the clear winner. They have the data, the search, and have the history/institutional expertise - Deep Mind one of the OGs of AI. They also have Waymo and other kickers.

-Apple - Up because they aren't going crazy on CapEx. A partnership with Google does the job; just like it did on Safari, it will on Siri. Also another plus for Goog.

-MSFT - Down because a decent amount of its runup was connected to OpenAI.

Is the Federal Reserve Unconstitutional? 

Part of the current case heading to the Supreme Court regarding tariffs revolves around Congress’s ability to delegate a Constitutionally given power, namely the power “To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises" as given in the first clause of Article I, Section 8.

However, in the fifth clause of that exact same Article and Section, it also gives Congress the power “to coin money” and “regulate the Value thereof.” Indeed, the Supreme Court has also previously interpreted Congress's power "to coin Money" as granting it the authority to regulate all aspects of the nation's currency, including paper money, during a series of cases from the late 1800s known as the Legal Tender Cases. 

So, if Congress cannot delegate its taxing authority, does that also mean it can’t delegate its monetary authority? And if so, is the Federal Reserve, by extension, unconstitutional as well? Something to consider as the tariffs case proceeds.

An excerpt from Jackson's Bank Veto Message of 1832 (more complete text linked below):

"The Congress, the Executive, and the Court must each for itself be guided by its own opinion of the Constitution. Each public officer who takes an oath to support the Constitution swears that he will support it as he understands it, and not as it is understood by others. It is as much the duty of the House of Representatives, of the Senate, and of the President to decide upon the constitutionality of any bill or resolution which may be presented to them for passage or approval as it is of the supreme judges when it may be brought before them for judicial decision. The opinion of the judges has no more authority over Congress than the opinion of Congress has over the judges, and on that point the President is independent of both. The authority of the Supreme Court must not, therefore, be permitted to control the Congress or the Executive when acting in their legislative capacities, but to have only such influence as the force of their reasoning may deserve."

Min filosofi är en rejält koncentrerad portfölj med mycket smalare utfall där väldigt få förväntas vara riktigt dåliga (pga att jag köpt så billigt att även ett dåligt utfall inte blir avkastningsmässig katastrof).

I exempel 1 så är det vanligaste utfallet förlust och i exempel 2 är det vanligaste utfallet vinst, även om snittet över väldigt stora tidsserier blir samma. Frågan är kanske om man någonsin klarar av att hitta tillräckligt många av exempel 1 för att nå till de stora talens lag?
Tråkiga aktier har däremot ett mycket snävare utfallsspann och därför kan en "tråkig" portfölj tåla en mycket högre koncentration.

På pappret är båda aktierna värda 100 kr. Problemet är att en portfölj med binära utfall får extrem varians och kräver att du spelar med de stora talens lag. Du måste helt enkelt ha många för att det förväntade värdet ska förväntas bli av i genomsnitt.

Exempel 2: Dagligvarukedja med 100 års historik
- 70 % chans på 96 kr
- 15 % chans på 50 kr
- 15% chans på 170 kr
= Förväntat värde 100 kr

Allt som oftast går det ganska bra. Ibland går det dåligt och ibland bättre, men det havererar aldrig.

Exempel 1: Biotech med "blockbuster-potential"
- 5 % chans på 2000 kr
- 95 % chans på 0 kr
= Förväntat värde 100 kr

Allt som oftast går det åt helvete, men nån gång ibland vinner man tillbaka allt och lite till.
Två case kan i grunden se helt identiska ut i förväntat värde men kräva helt olika portföljtänk för att man inte ska riskera att gå i konkurs. Låt mig ge 2 exempel.

På förekommen anledning (Neonode-tvistens utfall) har jag fått några tankar om diversifiering och värdeviktning av aktier. Spoiler: Alla sannolikhetsviktade värden är inte skapade lika. Utfallsspannet spelar enorm roll för diversifieringsbehovet.

@slackercapital Don’t forget about housing. Boomers are depending on it. We have to keep that pumped too. Otherwise, if housing, stocks and bonds all collapse, it’s lights out for banks and the global economy. Maybe leads to WWIII. It’s a monetary Hail Mary. Not saying it’s right. Just what I see coming to a central bank near you.

Without lower rates across the curve, the fiscal path of the US is dire. With lower rates, it is not ideal, but manageable. The question is can we do it without blowing up inflation. MMT would suggest we can. I think one way or the other, we are going to find out. 

It's a monetary gamble, perhaps a desperate one, but I think that not only the US and the Fed, but eventually the ECB and other major central banks around the world are going to join in on a global experiment of "lower for longer" despite inflation staying stubbornly above 2%. They will pin their hopes to a cocktail of MMT & AI deflationary forces. 

Case in point: In 2008, interest expense as a % of GDP was 1.7%. In 2020, it was 1.6%, a slight decline. Yet debt to GDP increased from 64.2% to 132.8% over that same period.

In 2021, interest expense was down to 1.49% of GDP and then doubled to roughly 3% despite debt/GDP staying relatively flat around 120%.

There's only two ways to bring down interest expense as a % of GDP: less debt or lower rates. My guess is that politicians from Rome to DC to Tokyo to London to Madrid and Paris are going to see lower rates as their only lifeline, eventually. 

Note: We basically spent 1985-1996 at 3% of GDP interest expense. The S&P went from roughly 167 to 740 during that time, an increase of 343%.

I could be totally wrong about this, but for the record, here's what I'm seeing and here's why I've been buying gold, TLT, SPY, etc.

Bonds seem to be capitulating today to a future MMT-Fed controlled by DJT appointees that will force short-end rates down for an extended period of time. 

The evidence is the break lower in 10yr yields. 

The talking heads like to talk about how the long-end isn't controlled by the Fed. Let me explain why I disagree.

Ultimately and historically, the Fed responds on the short-end with a reaction function correlated to NGDP. This leads the long-end to price based on long-run expectations of NGDP which are of course a combo of inflation and real-growth.

However, this is fundamentally a secondary and anecdotal reaction function that has historically been taken for granted b/c the supposition is that short-end rates will correspond to NGDP expectations.

HOWEVER, if you presume that front-end rates will not respond higher b/c of higher NGDP, then you must go back to the ultimate and primary pricing mechanism of longer-term rates, which is a discounted sum of short-term rates. 

Once the market believes that short-term rates will not respond as historically has been the case (according to NGDP), it must, ultimately and reluctantly, begin to revert to its primary pricing mechanism which is a sum of short-term rates.

Bond market beginning, but just barely, to believe today that short-term rates are going to stay lower for longer (regardless of NGDP) and are beginning to price in the longer-end accordingly. 

This is a flattening, not a steeping that has been all the rage to talk about lately. 

We are heading toward a flatter and lower curve.

Text from the Full Employment and Balanced Growth Act of 1978 is interesting at this point in time. It directs the Fed to seek both 3% unemployment and 3% inflation. It is the only time that I know of where Congress passed into law a specific inflation target.

Granted, it was just for the initial 5-year period after passing the law and it was later amended not to include a specific target. But nonetheless. It is interesting.

As most central bank watchers know, the current 2% target is not mandated by law and comes from actions that the New Zealand central bank did decades ago. 

The only inflation target Congress has ever given/alluded to is 3%, with a 3% unemployment target.

And, and this is key language quoted here, the "policies and programs for reducing the rate of inflation shall be designed so as not to impede achievement of the goals and timetables specified in clause (1) of this subsection for the reduction of unemployment."

In other words, Congress mandated the Fed to get unemployment down to 3% with 3% inflation. However, if those goals come in conflict, disregard inflation and focus on employment.

Says a lot, don't you think?

If Jim is correct, then native-born workers should not be seeing a significant increase in unemployment rate.

But they are.

Indeed, the only reason why the employment rate is steady at 4.2 is because so many immigrants have been deported/not coming, that jobs they typically fill are desperately looking to hire. 

Here's the proof. In July of 2024, the unemployment rate for foreign-born was 4.7%. It is now 4.1% and driving down the overall unemployment rate.

In July of 2023, the unemployment rate for native-born was 3.8%. It is now 4.7%.

I could also talk about the employment situation for recent college grads which is also anemic. 

Jim is a great macro thinker, but him calling JP out as caving and stating the employment situation in this country is very strong is simply dead wrong IMHO.

AI, he also claims optimistically, will be a strong driver of job growth in the long-run. Perhaps. But in the short-run, it will destroy jobs, especially for entry level. 

My views on the Fed and on Fed Funds are nuanced. So I don't think that the traditional transfer mechanisms from lower rates actually exist. But I think to claim Powell is caving, making a mistake, and that the labor market is strong is simply dead wrong.

This last post reminded me of my vagabond poet days in the late 90s/early 2000s. If anyone is interested, here's a few poems I wrote back then. Surprised I still had them in an old email that I sent to myself long after I wrote them. 

I was a much "deeper" guy in my 20s, but found it to be an evolutionary advantage to disregard all the truly important philosophical questions of life and focus on what's for dinner. 😉

"Slumber"

Falling from glorious cliffs,
Tumbling headfirst to the
Rocky valley below,
I hit my head upon the
Way and woke from
An unearthly dream.
Oxygen rushes back,
Senses quicken,
Yet calm breath
Betrays my gratitude
For being alive.
Searching high up on
The pristine peaks
Of wild ecstasy,
I could not find
My elusive quarry.
Down below, in the
Cactus and rock covered valley,
I lay sprawled,
Sprawled in an
Overwhelming abundance
Of just that which
I was searching for.

3.2.3

"Desert"

Trembling fear shakes the body
& wakes the soul into tomorrow.
Yet endurance builds and
Though the road gets steeper
& the path gets harder
We climb.
We climb.
We climb into atmospheric
Heights of carnal bliss--
Unadulterated vice growing
Eagerly in a palm oasis.
Under the weeds and grass,
Worms burrow their way
Into the never-ending night
Of the cold, dry desert ground.
Passing under cacti & jackrabbits,
They make their way, silently,
Like limbless ghosts
Crawling into oblivion.
Dancing in the distress
Of unfulfilled dreams
And living nightmares.
We too struggle to pass the test
And fall 6 feet into eternity--away--
Away from the nagging gap
Between God and man.

6.26.3

"Complaints"

Carpets & rugs are all
To be seen as I
Walk over the
Madness & mayhem of
God’s sense of humor.
Stinking up the place,
Like gym socks &
Jock straps, we creep
And crawl our way
Though the labyrinth of life.
Looking for the cheese
At the end of the puzzle,
What we find instead is
A note from the manufacturer:
“Thanks for playing, but
Sorry, this piece is not
An instant winner,”
Not a ticket to paradise
First class but a
One-way Greyhound bus pass
to a town
Outside of Boise, called
Nowhere.

If you want to learns something about how Social Security is funded, read this:

Trump signed an EO today regarding social security. I think it is so funny and ridiculous how the media is using it as an opportunity to talk about the "trust fund" running out of money soon. There is no trust fund. It is a fund filled with Treasury debt. 

Treasury redeems that debt on an ongoing basis already and then issues new public debt to make up the shortfall between incoming funds and outgoing payments. The fund is already insolvent and has been since 2020 when it began being run down. It reached a peak of $2.9 Trillion in 2020. Since then, it has been declining and the US has been issuing new publicly-held debt to fund the shortfall.

Works like this: SS goes to Treasury and redeems special issue Treasury bonds to make payments. Treasury goes to public markets to fund that redemption. There will be no step-up in publicly-held funding necessary when the "trust fund" goes dry. The shortfall is already being funded by newly issued publicly-held debt. 

We already fund any and all shortfall between incoming SS funds and outgoing payments with the issuance of new publicly-held debt. What we do is an accounting trick where we cancel out inter-governmental debt and then issue new publicly-held debt to pay the short fall. 

In other words, nothing magical will happen in 2033 or whenever SS "runs out." New publicly-held Treasury issuance will not change. For every $1 billion in short fall, we will issue $1 billion in new publicly-held debt, just as we already do. 

But we not be able to X-out $1 billion in debt on the balance sheet and make that new public debt neutral insofar as total US debt outstanding. Hence it's all accounting. Outstanding debt will increase, but new public debt issuance will not change by 1 cent. 

What we do need to do is amend the laws to make SS payable by new Treasury debt. It's already happening indirectly, but not allowed directly by statute in a technical sense. 

Do you really think Congress won't vote to keep things going as they already are to save SS? It will just make the total Outstanding debt of the Treasury increase on the balance sheet, but will not change, as I've said, by one cent, the amount of publicly-held debt that Treasury is already issuing. 

No one on TV or in the media really understands this. And very people anywhere else understand it either.

Some things to consider about the upcoming nomination from Trump for Kugler's vacant seat. 

If DJT wants someone to be chair next year who is not currently on the board, he has to nominate him/her for this vacancy. The new chair must be chosen from the board. Thus, if he wants Warsh to be the next chair, he must nominate him for this vacancy or take the chance that Powell does not resign as governor after his term as chair ends in May. Note, his term as governor does not end until after Trump's term ends (1/31/28).

Also note, the Kugler term is the only Governor opening scheduled for Trump's term. Hence, this could be his only shot to put someone on the board if Powell should decide to stay on. 

As a bit of irony, if Powell stays on after his term as chair expires, he would have precedent for doing so. This happened once before, when Marriner Eccles was not reappointed as Chair in 1948 but remained as a Governor until 1951. 

This is ironic for two reasons. 1) Eccles is who the Fed HQ building under scrutiny now is named after; and 2) during the period that Eccles served, the Fed basically answered to Treasury and was not independent. It did what FDR wanted to support the war, including yield curve control. 

All above said, I think Powell will resign as governor in May. Why would he put himself through more of this? So it's likely Trump will put in someone he thinks a possible chair, but if he doesn't like what he sees, he will get a do-over next year, or be able to elevate Waller to chair.

The US has gained an overall 139K unemployed people over the past year, but that number for native-born women has jumped by 252K. What is going on here?

In some ways, Table A-7 is the most important/telling Table from this month's jobs report. It shows a breakdown for four broad categories of workers: foreign-born men/women & native-born men/women. 

The unemployment rate for foreign-born men is unchanged YoY at 3.8%. It has declined from 5.8% to 4.4% for foreign-born women over the last year. Were it not for this dramatic decline, the overall unemployment rate would be much higher. Indeed, it is clear that immigration policies are what's keeping the unemployment rate so low. Just look at what's happen to the native born.

Native-born men have seen a small rise in unemployment YoY, from 4.4 to 4.5%, but the real change is for native-born women: increasing from 4.5% to 4.8%, a full 0.6% higher than the overall rate of 4.2% and a 0.5% jump from the reported 4.3% unemployment rate just last month. 

In fact, the number of unemployed native-born women has increased from 2.973 million to 3.225 million, a jump of 252,000 over the past year. Over all groups, the number of unemployed has increased to 7.236 million vs. 7.097 million a year ago, or by 139,000. 

My take: Clearly immigration policy is skewing the unemployment lower by taking immigrants out of both the country as well as the tracking mechanisms. As for native-born women, my hunch is this has a lot to do with AI. 

Of all four groups, native-born women are the highest educated and most likely to be white-collar. We are seeing a much bigger/faster impact on the workforce by AI than the overall numbers suggest.
